title: A review of heat treatments applied to low and medium and high carbon steels used in cold drawn
abstract: Abstract Work hardening through Cold Draw (CD) in low and medium carbon steels is a field of growing interest in materials science, with significant applications in the power generation, nuclear, defense, military, and aerospace industries. Steel alloys modified through heat treatment and optimized by CD are at the core of modern industry. The reduction in machining costs and processing time achieved by obtaining a steel profile through near-net shape drawing and stretching it to a final form not only offers unique competitive advantages but also establishes the heat treatment techniques involved as essential for the future of economic development. This study aims to explore the role of flow stress in optimizing the Cold Draw process, emphasizing its impact on residual stresses and mechanical properties for high-performance applications, and how different heat treatment techniques affect the mechanical properties and performance of low, medium, and high carbon steels used in cold drawn processes.

sections.heading: Cold drawn steel and its relationship to different heat treatments
paragraphs: This work aims to be useful in understanding the effect of heat treatments on the microstructural modification that occurs during deformation hardening in cold drawn steel (CD), by combining documented knowledge from practical industry reports in cold steel processing with the latest materials technology information. It offers a cutting-edge approach to aspects that will be useful in the optimization of industrial processes in the steel sector. The objective of this review is to analyze how flow stress parameters influence the optimization of Cold Draw processes, focusing on its stages and their effect on residual stresses and mechanical properties. Additional this article aims to provide an overview of the impact of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of low, medium, and high carbon steels, with a focus on optimizing cold drawn processes for industrial applications.

Cold drawing (CD) is a natural alternative to techniques like Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS), and the variety of complex shapes that can be cold drawn presents a direct benefit over material deposition technologies, especially due to the high strength that can be achieved from solidified steel that is then cold drawn. The applications are also numerous in the nuclear plant construction industry [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13 ].

In the physical phenomenon of cold drawing, a steel bar is deformed by local shear stress at the contact point, where sliding friction occurs between the exposed surfaces of the steel and the inner faces of the die. This causes local deformation in the contact areas and leads to nonlinear effects and regions of high strain, where the local shear stress at the contact generated is not proportional to the yield stress. The plastic drag that occurs when cold drawing the steel, after it has been annealed, is understood as flow stress, which is the stress required to continue plastically deforming the steel at a constant strain rate. Although the local shear stress generated on the contact surface does not significantly alter the internal profile of the steel, it does cause a surface modification that induces plastic effects on the external profile. This process results in controlled deformation of the steel. As the steel passes through the die and emerges from the other end, a reduction in the cross-sectional area of the bar is achieved, demonstrating effective plastic deformation. Due to the area reduction in the steel bar, the mechanical properties increase through microstructure refinement and cold work hardening [ 14 ]. See Fig.  1 . Represents a diagram of how the cold drawing operation of steel occurs, highlighting the areas of contact and frictional sliding. Fig. 1 Schematic of cold drawing and the microstructural evolution of steel

In the microstructure of steel, grain refinement occurs, where with each drawing, the grain becomes finer due to the accumulation of internal energy, which produces two phenomena during processing: annealing has a significant impact on the Jominy position 1/16—3/16, and this effect promotes the plastic behavior of the steel. The grain refinement starts from the plane normal to the surface and propagates toward the core of the steel.

During this process, two distinct phenomena are observed: by annealing and repeatedly cold drawing the steel, it gradually loses its hardening capacity, relevant to the cold work hardening mechanism and related to the bainite, ferrite, and pearlite phases. As the flow stress limit is approached and the steel’s brittleness increases, the cold hardening capacity will decrease. This is understood by the transition and rearrangement of the microstructural phases present. When annealing, the austenite phase with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure available in the steel will transform into phases such as bainite, ferrite, and pearlite, depending on the chemical composition and cooling rate. Annealing promotes the transformation of residual austenite from the hot rolling processes, improving the microstructural stability for cold drawing. Subsequently, in industry, a profile in physical and surface condition C4, annealed—cold finished (drawn), can be thermally treated to regenerate austenite by heating above the critical temperature and quickly cooling to produce martensite with a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structure. Austenite is an intermediate and essential phase for the formation of martensite, which imparts high hardness to the steel. Miller et al., have suggested that the identification of austenite should be performed by X-ray diffraction [ 15 ].

Meysami et al., have reported that the tempered martensite phase has formability and ductility similar to the ferrite-pearlite and bainite phases, which, in terms of cold drawing (CD), will not impact the reduction of the cross-sectional area of a steel bar through CD, concluding that ductility is similar across phases [ 16 ]. This is applied in the industry in 4140 Q&T alloys, which, after being hardened through heat treatment (HT) and exhibiting martensite, are successfully cold drawn to achieve exceptional surface quality. Industrial applications for cold drawn 1045 steel require a uniform lamellar pearlite and ferrite microstructure, which ensures a homogeneous distribution of mechanical properties along the profile, resulting in consistent strength and ductility, crucial for applications where high performance is required. The combination of lamellar pearlite and ferrite in the microstructure optimizes machinability of 1045 steel. On one hand, ferrite provides ductility and smoothness during machining, while pearlite adds the necessary hardness to maintain precise tolerances without compromising the structural integrity of components. See Fig.  2 Fig. 2 Microstructure in 1045 steel, 1000X, illustrating a predominantly ferritic microstructure with a smaller amount of fine pearlite, according to ASTM E3-11(2017), in a Cold Drawn RCS Bar

This microstructure can be further hardened in thermal treatments such as normalizing, induction hardening, and quenching and tempering. When normalizing, the grain distribution is further refined, internal stresses are eliminated, and toughness is improved, making it ideal for applications requiring a balance between strength and ductility. Induction hardening is particularly favorable for lamellar pearlite, as it is essentially a mixture of ferrite and cementite, responding quickly to heating, forming a martensitic surface layer while maintaining a ductile core.

This grade is highly recommended for the manufacturing of shafts, gears, and applications requiring high surface wear resistance with an impact-resistant interior. Quenching and tempering in 1045 steel will result in a phase transformation to martensite upon rapid cooling, with subsequent tempering providing excellent durability.

Increasing strength and hardness through cold deformation depends on three aspects: thermochemistry, metallurgy, and manufacturing. This relationship is dependent on the plasticity that can be achieved for each steel, and it is partially regulated by the grain size. Grain size is related to influencing properties such as ductility and strength [ 15 ]. The geometric and final tolerances of a profile in CD condition depend on the ability to control distortion from heat treatment (HT) and the deformation resulting from the cold drawing method on the CD bench. The flow of steel through the die requires a conical adjustment that must be calibrated to minimize torsion, and the surface condition is imperative. Phases such as bainite, ferrite, and pearlite experience minimal volumetric expansion during their formation, while the formation of the martensitic phase involves a significant volumetric change that causes distortion. Therefore, when seeking high hardness, the martensitic phase will induce distortions that can be balanced by precisely controlling the cooling process, in addition to complementing the steel's thermal state with stress relief.

Precise control over non-metallic inclusions, decarburization, and macro–micro etching are the result of prior work that involves relating the reduction in the area of a profile with the hardness gain at each step of the CD process, while annealing the steel without altering the delicate balance between the microstructural phases that regulate each of the steel's properties. It should be noted that during the heat treatment process and CD, tensile strength, impact energy, and hardenability may be modified [ 17 ].

CD directly involves the flow stress phenomenon, where Herbert Hollomon Jr.'s equation explains the behavior of steel and has been the basis for current mathematical models that allow for approximate calculations of final mechanical properties. The description of heat treatment at a certain temperature and defined time has an effect on steel, which is mathematically expressed by the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter. To relate changes in temperature or strain rate with the stress–strain behavior of a material, the Zener-Hollomon parameter is commonly used.

An estimation of the mechanical properties based on the strain hardening coefficient using dislocation theory is not recommended due to the number of variables that would need to be mathematically expressed. This is because they stem from quantitative models and depend on a large number of variables. Neves et al., reported an isotropic strain-hardening material model where they consider Coulomb friction, a cylindrical stress state, and Tresca's flow rule [ 28 ]. Aung & Ma et al., reported a constitutive model to characterize the behavior of anisotropic hardening in steel alloys subjected to plastic deformation, using the Hill48 element [ 29 ]. This model is applicable to the cold drawing (CD) process and demonstrates that crystalline plasticity models simulate dislocation mechanics at the grain level, which can help predict the stress–strain response [ 7 ,  30 ].

The theory in physical metallurgy and crystalline plasticity suggests that nanometric-scale crystalline deformation in a steel bar is not erased and the dislocation density cannot be assumed to be reversible, as proposed by Kitayama & Rauch [ 31 ]. On the contrary, dislocations in steel only reorient in a different crystallographic plane and direction; often, their size decreases, but they are not erased or reversed. Fan et al., have conducted a Fourier X-ray line analysis to determine the dislocation density in cold-drawn steel, reporting the evolution of dislocation density [ 32 ].

The CD process requires the annealing of a steel bar and then hardening it by passing it cold through a die, modifying its geometry into countless shapes. This involves the phenomenon of high-velocity shaping, leading to the formation of shear bands that increase the hardness of the steel, as the deformed bands resulting from plastic deformation in the steel induce microstructural changes, such as grain orientation and dislocations. Toribio et al., have shown that pearlitic colonies in steels tend to thin and simultaneously orient according to the axial direction in which the steel is drawn during the CD process [ 33 ,  34 ]. Toribio et al., have reported that CD produces a rotation of the lamellar pearlitic colonies, creating different crystallographic orientations in the colonies derived from the previous austenite grains [ 35 ]. Toribio et al., have reported that lamellar ferrite changes its orientation during cold drawing, as part of a colony and a set of lamellae, aligning in the direction of the cold drawing (CD) [ 36 ]. Bhattacharjee et al., have agreed with Toribio et al., on the orientation and alignment of pearlitic colonies; however, Bhattacharjee has reported the fragmentation and redistribution of cementite induced by deformation. In their discussion, they suggest that the reduction in the thickness of ferrite is greater than that of the cementite bands [ 37 ]. They consider the pearlitic colony as a critical fracture unit in cold drawing (CD), as within the same grain, the pearlitic colonies follow different orientation directions. They relate the elongated pearlite to microstructural fracture units. The deformed bands reflect the deformation of the steel under load conditions. Once the CD process is performed, the original microstructure of hot-rolled (HR) steel will be different. The deformed band indicates the level of deformation experienced by the steel and is a phenomenon related to CD. Jang et al., reported that the microstructure of cold-rolled steel after annealing corresponds to a recrystallized ferrite matrix and fine-grained austenite with a phase fraction of 25% to 35%, concluding that variations in annealing conditions affect tensile strength and elongation [ 38 ].

On the other hand, an empirical relationship would be: In a deformed band, there is no phase transformation, only plastic deformation, whereas in a transformed band, phase transformation occurs, leading to untempered martensite via austenite [ 39 ].

The nature of plastic deformation phenomena and phase transformation in steel are commonly misunderstood. There is certainly a tendency towards phase transformations in the heat treatment industry. A metastable phase formed by tempering steel from a high temperature creates a dense and distorted crystalline structure. As a result, the transformed band of untempered martensite can be extremely hard but also exhibit brittleness, leading to high surface hardness with greater susceptibility to fracture. Even so, the transformed band will be harder in terms of surface hardness when compared to the deformed band resulting from plastic deformation. A. Clarke et al., reported that at low tempering temperatures below 250 °C, carbon remains mobile, and the diffusivity of substitutional elements is still too low to influence the microstructure and substructure of martensite [ 40 ]. Lee et al., reported tempering conditions for 4340 steel where the strain exponent decreases with higher temperature and time [ 24 ]. The above, in terms of cold drawing (CD), will result in the steel not reaching maximum hardness during plastic deformation, improving formability while reducing the cross-section of a steel bar. In the CD process, this contributes to stabilizing low hardness while maintaining ductility and avoiding the risk of fracture. The temperature at which tempering is performed determines the distribution of carbides in the microstructure. In industry, CD is widely used over techniques like Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD), High-Pressure Torsion (HPT), Accumulated Roll Bonding (ARB), Ultrasonic Impact Treatment (UIT), and Equal Channel Angular Pressing (ECAP).

Today, major steel mills produce hot-rolled (HR) steel and work with metallurgical and casting practices aimed at homogenizing the microstructure and delivering refined grains to optimize steel properties. Thus, the size of the casting bloom is important for the CD process, as after casting, a bloom is formed, followed by a hot-rolling process that reduces the cross-sectional size to billet dimensions. For the CD process, a refined grain size of 8–10 tends to complicate plastic deformation. Analyzing this through flow stress terms and concepts, fine-grain casting practices combined with the aggressive area reduction between Bloom and billet have been studied to determine the ideal relationship between casting and rolling processes, such as when starting with a Bottom Poured Ingot and hot-rolling it to a Billet Ingot. Processes like Strand Cast-Vertical, where an ingot is rolled, result in an area reduction of 527.98:1, and the resulting grain structure does not allow the necessary plastic deformation for the flow stress of the steel to permit the CD process to occur. In the case of 4340 steel, due to specifications like DMS-1555 Grade B, an alternative is spheroidized annealing via HT to soften the steel, which significantly increases the cooling time. Coarse grain practices have been recommended, which would force the aluminum content to a low limit between 0.003 and 0.005, allowing preferential coarse grains for cold drawing. Dobrzanski et al., reported that the decrease in flow stress is linked to the course of dynamic recrystallization during hot plastic deformation [ 41 ,  42 ]

The plastic deformation that occurs in cold drawing (CD) is due to the sliding of linear dislocations in the crystalline structure of steel. These dislocations reorient when a local contact stress is applied. The movement of dislocations is limited due to the low temperature of the steel, which results in increased resistance. The accumulation of dislocations and linear defects in the crystalline structure optimizes the properties, which is brought about by the introduction of the cold work hardening phenomenon. When this occurs, residual stresses are typically formed in the steel [ 4 ,  14 ,  43 ,  44 ]. This has a significant influence on dimensional stability. In cold drawing (CD), phase transformations are limited; however, some exceptions have been reported, such as partial phase transformations of retained austenite to martensite due to cold deformation. Xiaoping et al., reported a high-pressure quenching process that demonstrates the formation of martensite in sheets, with an increase in content as pressure increases. A low density of the grain boundaries of the sheets was observed. Additionally, ferromagnetic and paramagnetic spectra were reported, along with an incomplete transformation of austenite. Crystal lattice distortions were also observed to increase [ 45 ].

Bhadeshia et al., have reported that the defects in the bainite structure are attributed to the shear transformation mechanism [ 46 ]. Miller et al., reported that the deformation hardening of the constituent phase tends to decrease with a finer grain size, such as 8–9, which would hinder and reduce the flow stress during cold drawing (CD). The role of individual phases like ferrite and martensite will have a significant influence on the tensile strength [ 38 ]. It has been determined that using a grain size around 5 would offer the best results. Prasanna et al., reported that the martensitic fine grain structure transformed into a coarse grain structure during annealing, improving ductility and softness [ 47 ]. Martensite in the microstructure of steel increases the hardness to its highest point. Tempering is usually performed to add ductility by reducing residual stresses without altering the morphology of the martensitic phase [ 24 ]. It is common for twinning hardening to occur during deformation hardening, forming crystalline twins in steel. This blocks the movement of dislocations and further strengthens the steel. The texture of cold drawing corresponds to the preferential alignment of the grains along the direction in which the cold drawing (CD) occurs. Mukherjee et al., have reported that martensitic steels exhibit grain growth along the preferential solidification direction 〈001〉 [ 48 ,  49 ]. The texture modifies the material properties, and these changes stem from the material's anisotropy. Rowe et al., reported that 3 wt% silicon in an iron alloy will develop a texture that increases the magnetic permeability of the steel in the rolling direction [ 50 ]. Liu et al., reported that during cold rolling at low deformation followed by annealing, there is a reduction in surface roughness, and the deformation corresponds to the different differentiated phases [ 51 ]. Annealing improves magnetic properties by reducing the size of smaller grains and relieving residual stresses in the material. Nebbar et al., reported the evolution of the microstructure in a cold-drawn wire, where elongation is induced in the grain direction, and a < 110 > fiber texture develops parallel to the wire axis [ 52 ,  53 ]. This same direction is created in cold-drawn steel bars with a ferritic matrix. A common practice in cold drawing is to perform demagnetization below 20 A/cm. Strain hardening is directly related to cold drawing, where the reduction of area in a steel bar leads to an increase in dislocations, improving mechanical strength. The grain morphology is affected by plastic deformation, resulting in sub-granular structures within the original grains due to the division caused by the pressure exerted on the steel bar. Lee et al., differentiated between the microstructural morphology of martensite from low and high carbon steels, relating lamellae grouped in large packets for low carbon and plates with twins for high carbon [ 24 ].

Another characteristic is the delayed recrystallization that occurs after cold drawing. This is because the material does not undergo complete recrystallization immediately; rather, the grain transformation occurs at a slower rate and at room temperature. Three factors are involved in this property: the steel composition, the amount of deformation, and the temperature–time. The chemical composition of the steel can hinder the minimum atomic mobility required for nucleation to transition to the growth of new grains, while the amount of cold deformation will produce delayed recrystallization, as the steel needs to rearrange atomically in terms of defect density and dislocations. Finally, temperature–time: the phenomenon is considered transient after cold drawing (CD) processing.

The benefits of delayed recrystallization include the partial restoration of ductility, reducing susceptibility to brittle fracture, and greater dimensional stability due to the presence of new grains that help reduce internal residual stresses. An important feature is the dynamic recrystallization that occurs after CD in a steel bar, where gradually the ambient temperature induces a slow migration of grain boundaries and leads to the nucleation of new grains in deformed areas. As the steel relaxes and stabilizes after CD, the grain boundaries move and recrystallize, balancing the steel and leaving it free of deformation. At the same time, the gradual reduction of internal residual stresses acting in compression helps balance and partially restore the crystal structure and ductility to the optimal point, evolving into stability and equilibrium over time. Ruslan et al., reported that the degree of stress relaxation depends on the heat treatment, stating that an increase in plastic deformation will increase stress relaxation [ 54 ]. When performing cold drawing (CD) on a steel bar, the plastic deformation is high and depends on the reduction in area. It is of interest to consider where the stress relaxation originates, as at the start of the CD process, a spheroidized annealing (SPH) will have a significant effect on the material's stress relaxation. Later, when cold work is done, part of that stress relaxation will be transferred, but in the CD condition, it will be less than in the annealed state, indicating that it originates during the heat treatment, as reported by Ruslan. Pragmatic experience has shown that the stress is relieved and hardness increases when a steel bar is cold drawn. It has been established that this is a beneficial effect, and the heat applied to the steel during heat treatment provides enough energy to continue with the recrystallization and grain refinement that was incomplete. This phenomenon is exemplified in the Hall–Petch relationship. Dobrzanski et al., have reported that transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP-type) steels consist of a multiphase structure of ferrite, bainite, and retained austenite [ 41 ]. Kaikkonen et al., have reported that, in medium-carbon steels, the ausforming process in primary martensite produces nanostructured bainite in a range of 660 °F with isothermal holding times of 60 min. Bainite/martensite formation is induced by deformation. At lower isothermal temperatures, bainite forms more rapidly [ 55 ,  56 ].

sections.heading: Effects of heat treatment on the microstructural transformation and properties of low, medium and high carbon steel alloys
paragraphs: The transformation of the microstructure of steel through heat treatment (HT) provides the ability to tailor the steel for different applications. Heat radically changes the nature and behavior of steel, and controlled heating rates are specified for each type of steel. While maintaining a constant temperature helps in microstructural homogenization and the definition of intermetallic phases, rapid vs. slow cooling also produces opposite effects, either refinement and hardening or, on the other hand, spheroidization and softening of the steel. Prasanna et al., have reported on the microstructural modification that occurs after performing vacuum heat treatment [ 47 ]. Zhao et al., have reported that the state of the austenite grains is crucial in the microstructural transformation and mechanical properties of alloyed steel during heat treatment and subsequent hot working [ 57 ]. In a cold-worked steel, the increase in hardness leads to a rise in dislocation density [ 58 ,  59 ]. This generates anisotropy in the BCC structure, which has multiple slip systems. The full tensor treatment shows that the activation of these systems is much more complex compared to the FCC structure. The multiple slip systems are specific to each of the grains, and each grain will have a different orientation. However, annealing in cold-drawn steel is crucial, as it reduces dislocation density and anisotropy, decreases hardness, and improves both ductility and toughness through recrystallization and the restoration of mobility in the slip systems, resulting in a more homogeneous and resilient material.

The kinetics of the microstructural transformation of a steel alloy has been linked to the chemical composition and austenite grain size. The critical temperatures of the transformation to austenite during heat treatment are represented by Ac1 and Ac3 for hypoeutectoid steels, and for hypereutectoid steels, Ac1 and Acm. The alloying elements substantially influence these critical temperatures, such as chromium (Cr), which raises the eutectoid temperature, while manganese (Mn) lowers it [ 60 ]. Chen et al., have reported the accelerated martensitic transformation and its effect on delamination fracture in 1050 steel [ 61 ]. Alloying elements such as Cu, Ni, Cr, Nb, V, and rare earths improve corrosion resistance in high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels. In particular, the addition of Cr and Ni significantly increases corrosion resistance [ 62 ]. In an annealing operation, the diffusion of atoms and relief of residual stresses lead to lamellar, pearlitic, and spheroidized annealing types.

The heat treatment equipment is crucial, with different types of furnaces providing various levels of incremental quality, ranging from open-hearth furnaces, atmospheric, vacuum, to ultra-high vacuum furnaces. The implications of using and selecting each furnace depend on the level of decarburization specified by the application. Marder et al., reported in a study the determination of the decarburization kinetics of Fe–C alloys, expressing values for a 0.1% C alloy as a function of time at 816 °C [ 63 ]. The control of oxidation and chemical reactions occurring on the steel surface must ensure the integrity of the steel.

The selection of an atmosphere for heat treatment (HT) should carefully consider the volume, velocity, composition, and purity of the gases, as it will have a significant impact on the steel's properties such as decarburization and corrosion resistance, in addition to safety considerations. The presence of decarburization can be evidenced with etching contrast, typically on the edge of a steel sample [ 64 ]. See Fig.  3  The significance of this image lies in demonstrating the formation of a thin decarburized layer during the vacuum annealing process in 8740 alloy steel. Fig. 3 Partial decarb according to ASTM E-1077-14(2021). Image of partial decarb obtained by vacuum annealing and nitrogen cooling

G.W. Simmons et al., have reported the kinetics of crack growth in 4340 steel in interaction with hydrogen, which has been related to an activation energy of 14.7 ± 2.9 kJ/mol, while in interaction with water, it is 33.5 ± 5.0 kJ/mol [ 65 ]. The crack propagation direction has been the same in both water and hydrogen according to fractographic evidence. However, the interaction mechanisms are different for steel-hydrogen gas and steel-water. In the steel-water relationship, there is a series of latent processes that need to be explained to understand the phenomenon. On the other hand, in hydrogen gas embrittlement, the activation energy should be higher compared to steel-water due to gas diffusion and the weakening of iron-iron bonds, resulting in increased susceptibility to fracture. However, in the steel-water interaction, embrittlement by hydrogen contained in the water will be less significant compared to hydrogen diffusion directly onto the material. This suggests that the activation energy is only higher in water due to additional processes requiring more energy, such as hydrolysis, corrosion, and the formation of hydrogen compounds. These associated processes can explain why water presents a higher activation energy. Gerberich et al., have reported the effects of hydrogen on crack growth rates in 4340, explaining the initiation site and diffusion [ 66 ,  67 ]. Goanță et al., have reported fine equiaxed grains due to recrystallization that occurs during fatigue testing. Intergranular fracture was reported due to micro-cracks between the grain boundaries [ 68 ]. Dobrzański et al., reported that it is possible to obtain a fine-grained structure before the solution heat treatment by controlling the dynamic and meta-dynamic recrystallization processes that occur during the hot-rolling process [ 16 ,  41 ]. Schöning et al., have outlined the interactions between the four physical fields of induction hardening: temperature, microstructure, stress–strain, and electromagnetic field [ 69 ]. The interactions between temperature and phase transformations are highlighted, along with latent heat of transformation, dilatational strains, transformation plasticity, and the dependence of microstructures on the electromagnetic field. Waechter et al., have reported that distortion is relieved in steel through residual stress relaxation, soaking time, recrystallization, and the volume change that occurs during induction hardening [ 70 ,  71 – 72 ]. The factors leading to inhomogeneity, increasing distortion in the thicker hardened layers, have been reported by Nunes et al., They state that distortion carriers take into account both the microstructure and the chemical composition [ 73 ].

Heat treatment is a complex field involving various sequences and stages that describe its nature: treating a metal with heat, maintaining it constant, and cooling it. There are mathematical equations used as models to represent the physical phenomena of each stage in different processes, such as diffusion, heat transfer, and phase transformations. Fick's diffusion equation is applied in carburizing and nitriding processes to predict how elements like carbon or nitrogen diffuse into the surface of steel, improving surface hardness. The Gibbs–Thomson equation relates the predominant phase size to the equilibrium temperature between phases, which is beneficial in precipitation processes and grain growth during annealing. It provides an understanding of how temperature influences the size of the secondary phase particles, offering a tool for controlling strength. Zhang et al., have reported that the size and distribution of precipitates in a microstructure can be affected by heat treatment. Additionally, carbide precipitates during tempering improve strength and modulate austenite stability to enhance toughness [ 6 ].

Increasing the temperature just before cold drawing increases the flow stress because it affects the strain rate. This implies that in cold drawing (CD), the flow stress will be more stable in terms of strain rate and temperature [ 74 ]. When performing cold drawing (CD), the strain rate should be decreased during the drawing process to avoid affecting the yield strength [ 75 ]. It has been published by A. Laasraoui et al., [ 19 ,  76 ]. The activation energy is a property dependent on the alloying elements. When diffusion of elements occurs in the crystal lattice structure under the original condition, these elements remain in the same position. However, during a cold drawing operation, there is a reordering of these elements at the surface. If, in addition, the material is heated just before being drawn, the activation energy will be higher, allowing the material to flow more freely. This supports the idea that it is possible to work with steel grades that exhibit high hardness and strength. Sajadifar et al., have reported dynamic recrystallization expressed in terms of flow stress, arguing that to reduce the flow stress value, the deformation temperature should be increased and the strain rate decreased [ 19 ,  77 ]. Sugino et al., reported the slip of grain boundaries as a result of dislocation movement. Due to the constraints of adjacent grains, the slip no longer progresses, as the stress concentrates at the triple grain junction, absorbing vacancies and rearranging, which decreases the dislocation density and induces dynamic recovery [ 78 ].

sections.heading: Advanced heat treatment and microstructural control in low and medium carbon steels for aerospace and high-performance applications
paragraphs: The production of low and medium carbon alloys involves electric arc furnace (EAF) casting processes that use techniques such as vacuum degassing to remove impurities from the molten metal and relieve pressure to evacuate dissolved gases in the crucible. This significantly contributes to the production of high-quality steel, for the formation of a billet up to 28 × 28″, which is then reduced in cross-section by hot rolling to 11 × 17″ into a billet, followed by subsequent rolling processes to reduce the cross-section of the ingot to manageable dimensions of solid bars, SBQ.

Certifying a grade under an aerospace specification requires compliance with rigorous testing to evaluate its properties, as well as certification by a regulatory entity to ensure that the necessary criteria have been met by an organization. Additionally, it guarantees the material’s quality and its suitability for specific applications. Straumal et al., have postulated that phase transformations enable mechanical design and heat treatment for property control [ 79 ].

Some of the most demanding certifications have included grain orientation in directions of interest for each application. When quenching is performed, the effect of component reorientation is also a crucial variable, as well as agitation, the quenching medium, and the fluid temperature. All of these factors have an impact on distortion control [ 80 ]. Mechanical properties can vary depending on the direction in which the tensile test is performed. This is because grain orientation is related to the steel's anisotropy. Mechanical properties are stronger in the direction where the preferential alignment of the grains predominates. When steel requires impact resistance and fatigue resistance, the grain orientation direction is specified.

Quenching involves rapidly cooling the steel from the austenitizing temperature to quenching in water, oil, or air, which has implications for the steel's hardness and brittleness. Lai et al., demonstrated an increase in the fracture toughness of a 4340 steel by raising the austenitizing temperature, which induces an increase in the amount of retained austenite and the elimination of twinned martensite [ 6 ,  81 ,  82 ]. Tempering aims to improve toughness and ductility. The atmosphere in which a heat treatment (HT) is performed is essential for controlling the quality of the steel and its properties. Fourier's equation is very helpful in showing the heat distribution of a mass of steel and how it is affected by transient effects. It is used in quenching and tempering to control the speed and uniformity of heating and cooling to prevent deformation and achieve a specific microstructure, quenching refers to rapid cooling, and tempering refers to the subsequent heating to reduce the excessive hardness acquired during quenching. The Johnson–Mehl–Avrami-Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation represents a kinetic model of the phase transformation for martensite, predicting the phase transformation percentage over time to optimize heat treatment time and temperature. Newton's cooling law describes the change in temperature as a function of time and its surroundings. It is applied in calculating the cooling rate for quenching and tempering and is commonly used to form exact martensite and avoid cracking or distortion.

The optimization of the mechanical properties after thermally treating an alloy has been a subject of recent study, such as wear resistance, following operations like quenching (Q), tempering (T), and cryo-treatment [ 83 ]. The hardness of steel after it has been quenching and tempering (Q&T) comes from the precipitation and dispersion of carbides [ 24 ]. Tang et al., have reported a procedure to achieve better grain refinement through rapid annealing. In this process, steel is quickly heated to the annealing temperature by induction, where grain recrystallization plays a dominant role due to the rapid heating [ 84 ,  85 ]. Mohrbacher et al., have investigated a steel with Mo that has been treated with a recovery annealing process, showing an ultrafine grain microstructure ranging from 0.5 to 1 µm, which improves strength. They report that recrystallization is recovered through the precipitation of niobium carbide nanoparticles. They have stated that the ferrite-cementite microstructure in the recovery annealing condition achieves ultrafine grain sizes and emphasize that niobium and molybdenum have a strong effect when in the solid solution state. Additionally, they discuss the role of Mo in preventing precipitation in low-carbon steels, improving processing through recovery annealing [ 86 ].

The use of Mo is understood as a stabilizer of austenite. However, the control of precipitates from undesirable elements must be carefully managed. The temperature and time conditions applied during heat treatment are very specific, but if the effects of these unwanted elements are not properly considered, the mechanical properties may not be uniform.

This review highlights several practical challenges associated with the implementation of this treatment. First, it is essential to precisely control the annealing temperature and time, as small variations can alter the microstructure and properties of the material. Additionally, the formation and control of precipitates from undesirable elements is another significant challenge, as these can negatively affect mechanical properties if not properly managed. Optimizing the process for large-scale production also presents difficulties, as the exact conditions must be maintained uniformly across all pieces. Moreover, controlling the formation of undesired phases during cooling, especially in the intermediate temperature range, is crucial to avoid inconsistencies in properties. The homogenization of the microstructure throughout the entire piece is another challenge, as variations in grain distribution can influence material performance. Furthermore, the use of high-performance alloys, such as those including Mo and Nb, increases costs, which must be considered when designing production processes. Finally, the long-term behavior of the material, such as its resistance to fatigue and corrosion, must also be evaluated to ensure that the steel's properties remain consistent over time.

Jiang et al., have reported that the spacing between cementite layers in pearlite is critical for mechanical properties. By prolonging spheroidization in pearlite, results have shown that the material’s strength will not be lower than that of ferrite [ 87 ]. Nedjad et al., have reported that annealing steel at low intercritical temperatures will result in a significant increase in strain hardening [ 88 ]. This could provide a significant advantage in cold drawing (CD), especially in applications where subsequent induction hardening treatment is desired, as it would promote a better response to hardening. Thompson et al., investigated AISI 1045 steel using surface induction hardening treatment, finding microstructures formed from austenite with a grain size of 10 microns. To achieve a martensitic microstructure during induction hardening, the microstructure must first be transformed into austenite.

Lesyk et al., reported a study on AISI 1045 carbon steel hardened through laser heat treatment, where a specimen exhibited high wear resistance due to the formation of fine martensitic grains [ 89 ]. By applying induction tempering treatment, they produced a high level of softening in the martensite [ 90 ,  91 ]. Edun et al., reported that the high-temperature intercritical heat treatment creates dual-phase ferrite-martensite microstructures and achieves a balance in the steel's strength [ 92 ,  93 ,  94 – 95 ]. Tabernero et al., reported an ultra-fast heat treatment in low carbon steels within the intercritical temperature range, representing the evolution of austenite during isothermal holding at different intercritical temperatures. The highest temperature peak corresponded to the initial austenite fraction. They also reported that the temperature peak strongly affects the kinetics of austenite formation and its growth. Furthermore, they noted that the morphology of the ferritic matrix was altered by the temperature peak and soaking time [ 96 ].

Chakraborti et al., reported in their study the continuous effect of the ferrite-martensite phase, where nucleation indicates that ferrite-ferrite boundaries are sites that promote the initiation of phase transformations [ 97 ]. Guo et al., investigated the microstructure of a carbon steel with Mn, subjected to intercritical annealing, revealing a microduplex structure composed of ferrite, tempered martensite, and retained austenite films. The evolution of strain hardening and the retained austenite fraction create a region rich in Mn and Ni, which helps to homogenize elongation [ 94 ,  95 ,  98 ]. This approach is enriching for the current state of this research because it allows for higher deformations without causing steel fracture. It also indicates that the stress distribution will be improved, reducing concentration points and decreasing the risk of failure due to cyclic loading. Furthermore, the enrichment with Mn and Ni will extend durability, creating a synergistic effect where austenite can transform into martensite during deformation, absorbing energy and promoting uniformity in elongation.

Parsa et al., reported the austenitization process for a high-carbon steel, using a mathematical approach to estimate the activation energy, reporting phase transformation mechanisms and how they are attributed to boron, delaying nucleation at the grain boundaries [ 99 ]. Ma et al., reported the dominant phases for medium-carbon microalloyed steels cooled by air after being subjected to austenitization and oil quenching thermal treatment, as pearlitic and ferritic steels. They argued that the low hardness is attributed to retained austenite due to incomplete quenching and possibly decarburization [ 100 ].

Ruiz-Hervias et al., reported that a stabilization treatment has been successful in reducing the residual stresses produced by the axisymmetric stress state during the cold drawing process in the ferrite and cementite phases [ 101 ]. This treatment has shown a beneficial effect on relaxation and corrosion behavior by influencing textures and residual deformations. These results were obtained through neutron diffraction in pearlitic steel. Ivanisenko et al., reported a micro-refinement of ferrite as a result of the dissolution of the cementite phase present, which could help control the microstructure of carbon steels [ 102 ].

Sun et al., reported on the two-stage austempering processes, focusing their work on the kinetics of bainite transformation. They demonstrated the effects on wear resistance and fatigue life of nano-bainitic steel, suggesting that bainite with a high-volume fraction extends the bainitic transformation time [ 103 ]. This is relevant because it allows for the idealization of the two-stage austempering control for nano-structured steel. Borhani et al., reported that the austempering of 4130 steel shows a microstructural evolution where a long austempering time at high temperatures reduces strength and increases elongation [ 104 ]. Long et al., reported the evolution of the bainitic phase in the microstructure transformation through a crystallographic study of a medium-carbon, carbide-free bainitic steel [ 105 ].

Królicka et al., summarized that the stability of bainitic carbon steels is due to the constituents of the microstructure and their nanometric dimensions [ 106 ]. During the controlled cooling process, it is observed that the transformation rate accelerates the kinetics of bainite formation; when cooled at a moderate rate, the granular proportion of bainite decreases in the microstructure, and the bainite plates are refined. However, the study does not address relevant aspects regarding residual stresses in steel and how these are affected by controlled cooling, nor is it clear how this could be applied in the industry. Huang et al., have suggested that hardness in steels is a consequence of the reduction of available intergranular and intragranular defects, particularly when the presence of solute segregation or impurities exists at the grain boundaries [ 79 ,  107 ].

Edun et al., have reported that carburizing heat treatment is the most promising among conventional treatments, as the atoms are able to diffuse into the crystal lattice of low-carbon steel, generating stress and improving the mechanical properties. This technique leads to the homogeneous dispersion of carbon particles in an ultrafine-grain martensitic matrix [ 92 ].

Xu et al., have reported the result of a quenching and partitioning treatment on a medium-carbon steel with Mn, where the morphology of the martensite and the constituents of the retained austenite were investigated [ 108 ,  109 ,  110 – 111 ]. What is relevant is that the predominant structure of the second phase evolves from large islands of M/RA in block form to a relatively fine morphology in the form of needles and grains.

Quenching is ideal for modifying the initial microstructure of steels. This process involves cooling the material after it has been heated. Each steel grade has a region in the iron phase diagram that shows the optimal temperature for quenching. Depending on the chemical composition, quenching can be done with different solutions, and many steel grades respond optimally to various mixtures [ 112 ]. Special attention must be given to the effects of distortion, resulting residual stress, and crack development during the process. Liu et al., reported on the influence of pre-torsion causing deformation on microstructures, which can lead to a reduction in mechanical properties [ 113 ].

Dulucheanu et al., have presented valuable data on the intercritical quenching treatment, where the resistance is increased and the deformability of dual-phase steels is reduced [ 114 ]. This is due to the volumetric fraction of martensite and ferrite in the microhardness of the structures. Tabernero et al., have determined that the soaking time in carbon steels increases the ultimate tensile strength, and this depends on the evolution of the volumetric fraction of the carbon content and the martensitic phase ratio, as well as how the ferrite recovers and recrystallizes and the size of the microconstituents [ 72 ]. The cooling that occurs during quenching forms the martensitic phase, which, together with the grain orientation, influences the nucleation and growth of martensite, controlling the volumetric expansion of the phase and distributing hardness in the microstructure. Subsequently, tempering will relieve internal stresses, allowing for a readjustment of grain orientation and improving toughness with little loss of hardness. The crystalline texture is also induced due to the alignment of crystal planes during rapid cooling. The crystalline texture is beneficial when high dislocation density planes are present, as this improves resistance to slip.

The effect on the refined microstructure in a steel that has been processed by cold drawing (CD) before quenching and tempering is critical, as the refined grain orientation with a well-aligned crystalline texture will optimize mechanical properties. Leijun et al., found that steel exposed to 40 years of service significantly strengthened, but showed slight embrittlement [ 115 ]. Wang et al., have reported on the impact of the austenitizing temperature required for martensitic transformation, correlating the 24 crystallographic variants of martensite with the K-S relationships of the transformation from the same austenitic grain. They found that the dislocation density increased with a higher austenitizing temperature, which is relevant in applications of pressure vessels in the nuclear industry [ 116 ,  117 ,  118 ,  119 – 120 ].

Bazri et al., have presented a study on the susceptibility to intergranular corrosion at the grain boundaries of a low-carbon alloy processed through CD, which shows evidence of high texture, linked to uniaxially deformed grains [ 121 ]. Masoumi et al., have proposed a heat treatment based on stages of cooling at different controlled rates, aiming to develop a complex microstructure that includes low bainite, proeutectoid ferrite, and pearlite in medium-carbon steels [ 122 ]. This process consists of austenitization, followed by a controlled temperature reduction to produce proeutectoid ferrite, then sustained cooling to complete the pearlitic transformation, and finally, gradual cooling to ensure the formation of bainite.
