sections.heading: Innovations in nanometric control of low and medium carbon steel alloys: effect of elements on the microstructure
paragraphs: The elements present in a steel alloy have the potential to significantly influence and modify the final properties of the steel, creating microstructural variations that alter the material's behavior during heat treatment. Zhang et al., have reported that the use of Nb, V, Ti, and Mo function as microalloying elements to refine the microstructure and promote precipitation hardening [ 6 ]. Nb segregates to the grain boundaries, while V forms carbides that restrict the growth of the austenitic phase grain. Elements like Ti and Mo act as grain refiners and improve toughness. The segregation of Mn at the grain boundaries typically leads to intergranular embrittlement, reducing ductility. Nano-precipitates prevent the diffusion of Mn, enhancing toughness and preventing embrittlement at those boundaries. Masoumi et al., have linked the high strength of steel 1070 to its high Mn content in the composition, while reporting that carbon contributes to the formation of coarse cementite [ 124 ]. Ran et al., have reported that vanadium carbide precipitates in spherical and nano-sized form within a carbon-rich martensitic microstructure improve strength by acting as blockers of dislocation movement, which hinders plastic deformation [ 125 ,  126 ]. Kaikkonen et al., have reported that steel alloyed with 1.5% Si delays carbide precipitation and its growth during isothermal holding [ 55 ]. Kaikkonen et al., have reported on the characteristics of bainite formation in medium-carbon steel, where the isothermal process was set at different temperatures to refine bainite at the nanostructure level and understand the role of Nb and Mo in transformation kinetics. They also reported the flow stress behavior depending on the deformation temperature, noting that as the temperature decreases, deformation-induced bainite transformation influences the flow stress below a strain of 0.3 at a strain rate of 0.1 s⁻ 1  [ 127 ,  128 ]. One of the points to discuss within this approach is how decisive temperature control can be in shaping the microstructure, especially compared to the cooling rate. Additionally, it would be beneficial to clarify how elements like Nb and Mo influence the microstructure at the nanoscale level, as this would enhance the understanding of bainite's role. From an industrial perspective, the applications of steels such as 4140 in quenching and tempering (Q&T) treatments, which require high strength and low ductility, provide a relevant context for assessing whether bainite-induced transformations could be advantageous.

Boutorabi et al., proposed a chemical composition for nanostructured bainitic steel with reduced density, reporting that Al and Co accelerate bainitic transformation while preventing carbide formation [ 129 ]. Their suggestion to replace Al with Si introduces significant economic considerations; however, the most intriguing impact lies in weight reduction. Furthermore, this phenomenon was also reported by Peng et al., and is attributed to dislocation strengthening [ 130 ]. Jiang et al., reported that nano-precipitates formed in the dislocation substructure of ferrite in a low-carbon alloy improve the steel's strength at the expense of plasticity. The addition of Ce leads to the formation of fine cementite particles within the matrix, which further contributes to the steel's strength [ 131 ]. This approach is highly interesting; however, it is unclear how the undesired effects of reduced plasticity, which may lead to increased alloy brittleness, are mitigated.

Rossi et al., reported that silicon (Si) and carbon content in steel stabilize retained austenite, increasing its quantity [ 132 ]. Kokkirala et al., have reported the role of retained austenite in the development of a nanostructured AISI 52100 steel [ 133 ]. Rossi et al., report that nanoindentation is the preferred method for evaluating hardness at the nanoscale, providing contrasting insights into microstructures and stress-induced transformations. Additionally, they highlight that phase relationships of individual microstructures in steel are not currently provided by steel manufacturers, identifying this as an industry gap. Franceschi et al., have reported methods to control carbide-free silicon-based bainitic steels, observing signs of carbon-enriched austenite in the form of films, demonstrating a high carbon content and a dislocation density of approximately 10 15  m⁻ 2  [ 134 ].

Fang et al., have reported the optimization of a wire produced by cold drawing (CD), nanometrically relating the thickness of microstructural lamellae to deformation. Although key details, such as the TEM images used to investigate interplanar spacing directly from diffraction patterns, are not shared, the authors present SAED images with a scale to reference how they correlated orientation with deformation [ 135 ]. Fang et al., have reported that when producing cold-drawn (CD) ultra-high strength pearlitic steel, a reduction in interlamellar spacing occurs, along with deformation of ferrite, resulting in an increase in dislocation density [ 136 ,  137 – 138 ]. Ray et al., have reported that the strength in ferrite-pearlite carbon steels depends on the constituent phases, which are governed by the ferrite grain size, while highlighting the interlamellar spacing of the pearlite [ 139 ]. Fang et al., have reported that CD steels, which typically exhibit a conventional pearlitic cementite microstructure, have been replaced by cementite nanoparticles bound by grain boundaries enriched with substitutional elements, resulting in CD steels with superior tensile strength and torsional ductility [ 140 ]. The lamellar cementite is in a spherical shape when heated above 400 °C. When annealed between 200–400°F, an amorphous transformation of cementite occurs, resulting in nano-crystalline grains. This transformation increases strength and ductility due to the formation of nanofilaments before the amorphous phase of cementite develops. It has also been reported that, with a carbon concentration of 17%, carbon-enriched regions promote the formation of nano-precipitates. By using low annealing temperatures, carbon segregation occurs, affecting intermediate carbides. In their experiment, Fang et al., report a carbon concentration of 12% and precipitate sizes ranging from 10 to 20 nm. Shi et al., have reported on a carbon steel (0.7–0.75%) in which nanotechnology was used to improve its mechanical properties through a CD process, achieving nano-grains of cementite via the deformation-induced mechanism of cementite flakes and nano-crystallization [ 141 ]. The drawbacks of nanotechnology in steels are that it could increase costs and process complexity. Nanostructuring is highly specific and may not be completely stable under different heat treatment conditions. Furthermore, the control and reproducibility of procedures to produce nano-grains can be susceptible to coarsening. Yang et al., reported colonies of randomly oriented pearlite with a fine interlamellar spacing of around 150 nm [ 142 ]. Additionally, they reported the effect of peak broadening caused by plastic and elastic deformations in the cold drawing (CD), which makes it difficult to identify residual stresses in lamellar cementite using X-ray diffraction [ 101 ].

Low and medium carbon alloys processed by cold drawing (CD) are important for the industry, and therefore, optimizing them using alloying elements to improve their properties is crucial. Some mills have reported coarse-grain practices by adding Ca and Si. Dong et al., presented an approach on how Ca and Zr improve the ductility of conventional steels through a technique used in casting to deoxidize the steel, improving the morphology of the inclusions to produce clean steel. This approach emphasizes the need to reduce the volumetric fraction of oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur inclusions. Speich et al., reported that the morphology of Type II MnS inclusions appears in flattened discs, with equal strains in each cross-rolling direction [ 143 ]. Temmel et al., reported that aluminum is used to deoxidize steel [ 144 ]. Garrison et al., have reported that the use of lanthanum improves fracture toughness in ultrahigh-strength steels [ 145 ]. Zhang et al., have reported that the addition of Si and V refines the grains and improves strength, toughness, and stress corrosion cracking resistance [ 6 ]. Toribio et al., observed how inclusions of MnS, Ti2O3, 2MnOSiO2, MnSiO3, TiN, and VN begin to nucleate, propagating microcracks in the pearlitic cold-drawn steel after passing through up to 4 dies. This is attributed to the transverse peripheral compression, and has an effect between the inclusion and the steel matrix, inducing a crack that magnifies as plastic deformation occurs [ 146 ,  147 ].

The 4340 alloy is a standard product that competes with modern ultrahigh-strength alloys. This conventional alloy has been optimized by Ganesh M. Kotiye et al., improving hardness and ductility by 15% and 55%, respectively. This has been made possible thanks to a cryogenic heat treatment [ 83 ]. Moreno et al., have published that annealing treatments relieve stresses and decrease fatigue strength, while normalizing increases fatigue strength [ 148 ,  149 ]. Arun Kumar et al., have proposed that 4340 does not show improvements in yield strength after bake hardening [ 75 ]. 4340 is sensitive to thermal changes in the process conditions, and this has a direct impact on the deformation rate [ 3 ]. Liu et al., have reported that when there is a change in the microstructure from granular bainite to acicular bainite, the increase in martensite-austenite constituents affects the plastic deformation behavior of the material, due to the increase in nickel [ 150 ]. Nickel has been associated with an increase in hardness and strength, as well as a reduction in ductility and the effect of hardenability. These effects have been related to 4340 steel.

Sharma et al., have determined the ideal spheroidization time for 4340 steel to be 9 h, during which cementite particles and spheroids are formed to improve ductility and machining properties. They have shown that after this time, continuous spheroidization will not make much difference in hardness, attributing that isothermal heating will not cause the annihilation of crystal imperfections [ 151 ]. Fang & Zhang et al., have reported that plastic deformation in cementite is limited to a length scale of less than 20 nm. This is relevant for cold drawing (CD) because cementite has been considered a phase that forms barriers and blocks dislocation movement. Since plastic deformation in cementite is limited, it can fracture and redistribute stresses in the material [ 152 ,  153 ]. A phase of cementite present in cold-drawn (CD) steel provides the necessary hardening mechanism for the steel. Toribio et al., have reported that cold-drawn (CD) steel improves fatigue resistance properties, as it blocks dislocation movement, which tends to delay the advancement of the plastic fatigue crack in the steel [ 153 ]. Fang et al., have proposed that the dislocation density in lamellar ferrite increases deformation during cold drawing (CD) [ 154 ]. Fang et al., found in their study that ferrite nano-lamellae, without cementite segregation, increase in thickness when subjected to cold drawing (CD) through grain boundary migration [ 155 ].

Caballero et al., have proposed medium carbon bainitic steels, in which the absence of precipitates is of interest to the industry [ 105 ,  106 ,  156 ]. By adding silicon (Si), cementite formation is inhibited, which is critical for bainite transformation. They have also reported that aluminum (Al) suppresses cementite precipitation from austenite. These studies focus on precipitation. Additionally, it has been reported that austenite in bainitic steels exhibits two different morphologies: in the form of films between ferrite bainitic laths and in blocks between bainitic sheaves. Although precipitation may be key, focusing on the suppression of cementite may have implications for toughness and wear resistance. Furthermore, the morphology of retained austenite is a critical factor. It would be interesting to explain how these differences affect the behavior of the steel under loading conditions. An explanation of the distribution of microstructural phases and their size could lead to further optimization. One of the perspectives for the cold drawing (CD) industry is medium carbon alloys.

My perspective in writing this review is the inclusion of the use of Mn and Cr, mainly in the distribution of cementite, creating a development line of 'Advanced Ferrite-Pearlite Steels with Hybrid Microstructure and Controlled Cementite', with higher strength and toughness. While precipitates, as suggested by Bhadeshia and Caballero, contribute to bainite phase stability, they isolate the potential of cementite, which, in metallic transformation processes and post-thermal treatments in industrial applications, is considered essential.

sections.heading: Defect factors and their impact on the mechanical properties of low and medium carbon alloys
paragraphs: During heat treatment (HT), alloying elements play a key role in the microstructure. Heat will modify the crystal lattice by rearranging the atoms in the steel. By maintaining a constant temperature, steel homogenization can be achieved through techniques such as isothermal treatment, where the steel is held at a constant temperature for an extended period to form a homogeneous microstructure, facilitating the relaxation of internal stresses that promote dimensional stability. These will then combine with the cooling method to achieve the desired characteristics. When a martensitic structure forms in the steel, it will experience generalized hardening due to the irregular arrangement of atoms in the crystal lattice, as atoms are trapped in a disordered arrangement, as well as the redistribution of carbon and carbide precipitation [ 157 ,  158 ]. Pohjonen et al., have reported the optimized temperature range with subsequent low-temperature isothermal holding for medium carbon content steels, where fine nano-structured bainitic lamellae of 100 nm are related to a hardness of 650 HV [ 159 ]. Seppälä et al., have presented a synthesis of the bainite growth model in medium and low carbon steels, where bainite growth begins at the grain boundaries of austenite, forming successive subunits that increase the thickness of the lamellae without extending their length [ 160 ]. Carbon quickly distributes to the adjacent areas, limiting longitudinal growth. Saeglitz et al., have reported that the crystalline structure of martensite is attributed to two fundamental processes during its formation. First, the high dislocation density induced by shear transformation from austenite to martensite, and second, a supersaturated lattice with carbon atoms as a result of the diffusion less transformation from austenite to martensite. These two processes cause carbon to be trapped in the octahedral interstitial sites, inducing tetragonality in the crystalline structure of martensite [ 161 ]. Alvarez et al., have introduced the concept that carbide-free, nanostructured bainitic steel has high abrasion resistance, which is attributed to the stress induced by martensite that hardens the surface [ 92 ,  162 ]. Jiang et al., have successfully optimized the isothermal treatment to produce nanoparticles that enhance the precipitation strengthening effect in steel, providing a comparison with microalloyed alloys containing carbonitrides [ 131 ]. The proposed approach is very good; however, the high-temperature stability of the nanoparticles deserves further study, as it will be important to understand how the nanoparticles affect ductility and what could balance this behavior to help accept this approach in future industrial applications.

Nedjad et al., have reported the existence of fine retained austenite particles at the grain boundaries of recrystallized ferrite, which is uncommon in low-carbon steels [ 88 ]. This raises an interesting discussion about the stability of austenite, as this phase can influence grain boundaries and modify toughness and strength. Additionally, retained austenite tends to transform into martensite under load due to energy absorption. Therefore, it is relevant to question how effectively it would transform into a low-carbon steel. Another implication is its influence on ductility: while it may improve, the impact on toughness will be less significant if the distribution is not optimal. Retained austenite could also compromise hardness and processability by introducing heterogeneity into the microstructure, so for applications requiring normalizing, achieving uniformity in properties would be challenging. Another aspect to consider is the impact of retained austenite on thermal stability, as at high temperatures, it could decompose and lose its effect on the final microstructure [ 11 ,  130 ,  163 ]. Hu et al., have explained the effect of retained austenite on fracture initiation, which preferentially occurs due to the blocking of the M + RA structure during crack propagation [ 164 ]. It has been reported that the Cr content is responsible for the hardenability of the 6150 alloy [ 165 ]. Xiang et al., have reported a method to control precipitates and solid solution strengthening, where Cr forms rich phases that enhance the yield strength by inhibiting the growth of precipitates such as M23C6 [ 166 ]. This is similar to the microstructure control that occurs during the CD process after heat treatment. Therefore, Cr-rich phases are located along the dendrite boundaries, influencing the nucleation of secondary phases. In cold drawing, these precipitates will have an effect depending on how they are distributed at the grain boundaries, affecting hardness and ductility. When nitrogen (N) is added, it inhibits the thickening of the precipitates. The limited solubility of N in the matrix leads to nucleation due to differences in the size and distribution of the phases.

Hernández et al., have reported heterogeneity in the microstructure of a Mo-enriched steel due to precipitates and intermetallic compounds that form during aging treatment, causing Mo depletion in the adjacent matrix [ 167 ]. Their approach is interesting; however, the depletion will lead to a reduction in mechanical properties, such as strength and hardness in certain regions, which is an undesirable effect. The microstructure will become more brittle due to the presence of intermetallic compounds, and the risk of microcracks in low toughness areas will become critical. Additionally, another factor to consider is the diffusion of Mo and its thermal stability, as at high temperatures, the precipitates may dissolve, affecting the durability of components subjected to load.

The proper heat treatment can improve the properties of a steel; however, it can have detrimental consequences if not carefully executed. Zhou et al., have reported residual stresses near the pearlitic microstructure in F + P, and in one region, a galvanic effect occurs between the ferrite matrix and the pearlite. These mechanisms explain the initiation of corrosion. Additionally, MnS inclusions leave pits after dissolution, causing pitting corrosion, according to the research reported in this study [ 168 ].

Decarb is one of the variables that requires the most care when working with aerospace-grade alloys. It is known that a flame exposed during heat treatment in the presence of oxygen will undermine the material's surface, reducing the surface carbon, which can lead to issues with the toughness of steel due to ferritic steel welds. Acicular ferrite positively influences toughness, as do oxygen and nitrogen [ 169 ,  170 ].

When normalizing, hardening, and quenching and tempering processes are executed, the brittleness of the steel and its ability to harden must be maintained in balance. Hardening processes involve rapid cooling in air, quenching in water, and quenching in oil, and these can lead to the magnification of defects present in the steel.

Special care must be taken to minimize the risk of fracture in steel due to inclusions that may be present in the casting, as these can escalate into cracks if they exceed the criteria set by ASTM E-45. Elements such as Al have been used in the steel casting industry to ensure that the chemistry meets the requirements for grain size. Dong et al., have reported that Al-Killed steel exhibits an inclusion structure consisting of titanium nitrides, stringer calcium, and manganese sulfides. It has been reported that MnS inclusions tend to elongate during hot rolling because they are softer than the matrix steel, and there has been a lack of correspondence between the in-plane anisotropy produced by MnS and the transverse ductility in the rolling direction, which increases the risk of failure [ 50 ,  144 ,  171 ,  172 ,  173 – 174 ]. The control of sulfide-type inclusions, along with low sulfur levels, allows for achieving reasonable toughness levels in ultrahigh-strength steels [ 145 ,  175 ]. Chaolei et al., have reported that fine compounds, MnS inclusions, induce the formation of intergranular ferrite in pearlitic steels [ 173 ]. Fan et al., have reported how Mn is used to improve the stability of austenite [ 176 ,  177 ]. Edun et al., reported that Mn forms weak carbides and tends to dissolve in cementite, reducing the carbon activity in austenite without forming its own carbides. When Cr is added, it induces Fe and Mn to replace carbon, forming alloyed cementite [ 92 ]. Fang et al., have investigated low-temperature annealing on the cementite structure, finding that annealing at 409.73 °F can transform the cementite in CD steel to its amorphous nanocrystalline state [ 178 ]. It is known that CD steels are sensitive to heat treatment, so a redistribution of carbon and partial dissolution of the cementite phase occur, affecting their mechanical properties. However, one of the most controversial questions about the reported finding is that, traditionally, the cementite phase in steels decomposes at higher temperatures, around 1292 °F. Therefore, logic suggests that the redistribution of carbon and partial dissolution of cementite would be limited. Regarding the statement about the nanocrystalline amorphous state, it is known that this would require extreme conditions and high-energy processes, and it is not explained in detail how this would occur.

Gündüz et al., have reported that in medium-carbon steels, austenite grains evolve into fine ferrite grains during cooling to room temperature, and although the strength is high, there is a drastic drop in elongation values when the steels are quenched in oil, due to the formation of fine ferrite and pearlite [ 179 ]. Chabicovsky et al., have identified that the cooling rate of steel treated by heat treatment (HT) must be carefully calculated and executed using the spray cooling technique [ 180 ]. In this process, determining the cooling rate is crucial, as the steel's microstructure is highly sensitive to thermal changes during the cooling stage. The cooling strategy depends on the shape and size of the part, while factors such as coolant pressure and flow rate are key determinants in the success of spray cooling. Additionally, parameters like water mass flux, water temperature, velocity, roughness, and droplet size are closely related to the formation of scale (oxide layer). The dispersion of fluids for cooling and the dispersion of hot vapors are essential to ensure a controlled transition to either a harder or softer steel, depending on the requirements, thus improving its final properties. Through metallurgy, the Continuous Cooling Transformation (CCT) can be determined for each case, adapting to the effects and specific purposes of each steel batch.

The risk of exceeding cleanliness values depends on a range of factors such as the part design and the residual stresses the material will be subjected to during the manufacturing process. Oxides, which are later classified based on their composition as sulfides, alumina, silicates, and globulars, begin their nucleation, generating microcracks present at the time of solidification. The orientation of these microcracks is a very important factor in understanding the origin of propagation, typically studied in fractography. Ruslan et al., have reported that the nucleation and propagation of microcracks in steel shorten its fatigue life [ 54 ]. Nunes et al., reported that surface residual stresses after cold drawing (CD) are strongly affected by local friction coefficients and slip-stick effects, showing a variation of a factor of 2 [ 181 ]. It has been reported by Ping Shen et al., that tellurium (Te) has been used as an additive to improve machinability in steel. It was also reported that the aspect ratio of 1–3 of the inclusion is an important parameter for the steel properties [ 170 ,  182 ]. Fu et al., have reported that Te modifies the morphology of MnS inclusions by reducing the sulfur content and decreasing the growth rate of the inclusions, thereby reducing deposition [ 170 ].

Yaguchi et al., have reported that the addition of Te globularizes MnS inclusions, improving machinability and evaluating it based on the cutting force required to remove chips [ 183 ]. Elements such as Manganese (Mn) have posed a challenge in terms of control when alloying with Te [ 184 ]. It has been reported that Type I manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions, in spherical form, result in better mechanical properties. However, Type II and III longitudinal MnS inclusions have been associated with lower mechanical properties [ 144 ,  185 ]. Additionally, rare earth elements (REE) act as grain boundary purifiers and contribute to controlling the morphology of sulfides.

Oxide inclusions, like sulfide inclusions, are used for steel refining, a technique known as "oxide metallurgy." Kimura et al., have highlighted the importance of controlling MnS precipitates [ 186 ]. Dong et al., have reported how deoxidation practices impact ductility and toughness. The inclusion density and chemical composition should be considered [ 171 ]. Grenoble et al., have reported that adding Mn to a steel alloy counteracts sulfur and reduces the inhibition of grain growth [ 50 ]. Lee et al., reported that the most common inclusions in AISI 4340 are MnS [ 24 ]. Shao et al., reported that MnS inclusions can be annealed through spheroidization; however, the evolution of an inclusion will cause the defect to grow [ 187 ].

By applying heat treatment, the activation energy will cause the grain boundaries to expand and recrystallize, leading to stress concentration and a reduction in the dynamic fatigue strength of the steel. Llorca et al., reported that the stress concentration present on the surfaces of steels leads to low cyclic stresses that initiate cracks, which are produced by inclusions, and have a detrimental effect on the fatigue limit of pearlitic steels [ 188 ]. Temmel et al., reported that with MnS inclusions, the fatigue behavior deteriorates as it induces anisotropy in the steel [ 144 ].

Cryderman et al., reported that MnS inclusions affect fatigue properties in the transverse direction to rolling in a medium-carbon steel [ 189 ]. Wang et al., reported a study on dynamic recrystallization that occurs when working steel with medium Mn at hot working temperatures [ 109 ,  190 ,  191 ]. But making a deep reflection and following the logic of the recrystallization theory, grain growth theory, and work hardening theory, a gap arises between what occurs in practice and classical theories.

In cold drawing (CD), when deforming the steel, the grain is refined without dynamic recrystallization, resulting in fragmented grains that will increase the steel's hardness. This contradicts classical theories, which associate grain refinement only with recrystallization processes that occur in hot working. Shen et al., have reported on primary recrystallization and phase transformation of austenite, which shows that ferrite exhibits less recrystallization with increasing temperature. Furthermore, in the two-phase region, the formation of austenite affects the morphology and size of the microstructure, inhibiting recrystallization and ferrite growth [ 192 ].

Figure  4  shows the variation of BHN hardness in relation to the chemical composition of 5 batches of 4340 steel, heat-treated by annealing at 1490°F, cooled in a furnace at 52°F/h until 671°F, and then air-cooled. The data was obtained from technical data sheets collected from matweb.com. Fig. 4 Variation of BHN hardness as a function of the chemical composition in heat-treated 4340 steel by annealing

sections.heading: Thermochemistry
paragraphs: In CD, thermochemistry is essential to understand the surface modification of low- and medium-carbon steels, from immersion in sulfuric acid to clean the steel of contaminants like oxides and scale, to immersion in soap and phosphate to form a lubrication layer, as well as carburizing and other processes like nitriding. It is important to consider how the steel's surface can be improved for its final application. Properties such as wear resistance and corrosion resistance are essential in the steel sector, and many applications require a surface roughness of 63 Ra micro-inches. Prasanna et al., reported that vacuum heat treatment has the ability to optimize the tribological properties on the steel surface [ 47 ]. While Amin et al., have presented an approach on acid solutions used in the steel industry, reporting the interactions between steel and sulfuric acid, using a cutting-edge method like electrochemistry with corrosion inhibitors based on organic compounds such as adenine, on low-carbon steel [ 193 ].

The evaluation of the effects of hot acid and soaking in liquid lubricants to clean and lubricate steel has shown a decrease in hardness due to the release of residual stresses present in the steel, as well as the migration of grain boundaries that will continue to move while the steel is soaked, due to the incomplete plastic deformation from the cold drawing (CD) process, which leaves some grains with enough energy to recrystallize. Toribio et al., have reported on the residual stresses and deformations present in the material, highlighting a key variable in process control: the relationship between the reduction in area and the level of stress and deformation resulting from the cold drawing (CD) process [ 194 ,  195 – 196 ]. These findings suggest the need to apply a stress relief treatment after CD operations involving significant area reduction, in order to minimize the adverse effects of accumulated residual stresses. Kumar et al., have reported on the importance of establishing friction conditions, due to the high pressure generated between the contact surfaces [ 197 ]. The influence of the lubricant and the type of reaction with the coating has been a subject of study, whether it is calcium-based or sodium-based lubrication with soap. This chemical reaction in both cases modifies the contact behavior between the die faces and the steel bars, altering the coefficient of friction and allowing the flow stress conditions to be optimized. Nishida et al., have reported on the distribution of internal residual stresses in a bar processed by cold drawing, showing the change in lattice-plane spacing in an undeformed sample [ 198 ]. Soap lubrication benefits the flow stress of steel by modifying the coefficient of friction, and it will have a direct impact on increasing tool life, as well as reducing energy consumption during cold drawing. Zhao et al., have reported that stress–strain is related to the flow stress of steel, explaining that the metal surface has less resistance to flow and is strongly deformed by frictional forces [ 199 ].

During the pickling of steel in sulfuric acid, some grades of steel, such as 4340, contain amounts of Cr and Ni, which complicate the removal of deposits such as scale and various oxide formations, including nickel oxide (NiO), nickel hydroxides (Ni(OH₂)), nickel sulfide (NiS), chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃), and chromium hydroxides (Cr(OH)₃), which can form during heat treatment. A common practice is the use of permic processes followed by sulfuric acid baths. The permic layer will facilitate the removal of scale and other compounds that need to be eliminated during pickling. Consideration should be given to adding corrosion inhibitors, complexing agents, and pickling accelerators as chemical agents to improve the surface cleanliness. Valarselvan et al., have reported on corrosion resistance using inhibitors in sulfuric acid, which form a protective film on the surface, allowing the corrosive effect of the sulfuric acid solution [ 200 ]. Xometl et al., have reported that the addition of imidazole-derived ionic liquids favors the reduction of hydrogen evolution in the cathodic regions and the dissolution of steel in the anodic region, contributing to a reduction in the corrosion rate of AISI 1018 steel. The trend in their experiments shows a decrease in the concentration of sulfuric acid, which is an effect of the inhibitor in the anodic regions [ 201 ]. Liu et al., reported a slightly different approach from Xometl et al.,, as they reported the use of an inhibitor such as hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) in a pickling process on carbon steel, and they reported the inhibitor's efficiency by increasing the immersion times and temperature [ 202 ]. Liu et al., reported the result of using an electrochemical method to prevent embrittlement in high-strength steels by removing the oxide from the surface using hydrochloric acid and employing ultrasound. They showed that steel 1062 can be pickled in hydrochloric acid without showing signs of embrittlement, as long as the reported electrical potential ranges are maintained during the pickling process [ 203 ]. El-Lateef et al., reported a MoS2 film, which is effective in preventing corrosion of C-steel in acidic solution [ 204 ].

To ensure an efficient and safe chemical pickling process with sulfuric acid, and to avoid the phenomenon known as “pickling burn,” it is essential to establish an equilibrium point that optimizes the concentration of sulfuric acid, dissolved iron, and the process temperature. The concentration of sulfuric acid should typically be maintained between 10 and 12% by weight, which is sufficient for effective pickling without being excessively aggressive, while the dissolved iron levels should remain below 2–3% to avoid secondary reactions and overheating. Figures  5  and  6  present an example of how to monitor two key variables in the pickling process. Figure  5  shows the sulfuric acid concentration over a month, while Fig.  6  shows the iron content monitored during the same period. It is important to note that these data are only a representative example of how values would appear in a process and do not represent data from any reported process. This analysis aims to develop a criterion or balance point for monitoring these variables. Fig. 5 Sulfuric acid concentration monthly monitoring Fig. 6 Iron content monthly monitoring

The bath temperature should be controlled around 158°F (70 °C) to achieve optimal efficiency in the reaction. Regular monitoring and adjustments of these parameters, along with proper agitation of the solution, ensure a uniform reaction and prevent localized hotspots or contaminant buildup. This allows for a balanced pickling process, minimizing risks and improving performance. However, it is crucial to establish clear criteria for when to use chemical pickling versus other surface treatment techniques, such as shot blasting. One of the main factors to consider is the nature of the surface contamination. If the contamination consists mainly of oxide scales, thick deposits, or other mechanical residues, shot blasting may be preferable, as it effectively removes coarse contaminants like scales. On the other hand, if the contamination is mainly oxide and other soluble chemicals, pickling may be more suitable, as the acidic solution efficiently dissolves these contaminants. Another important aspect is the size and nature of the coarse steel scales: if they are small enough for shot blasting to remove, this process is effective; however, if the scales are large or firmly adhered, shot blasting may not be sufficient, requiring additional treatment such as cutting or machining, or pickling would be more appropriate. Furthermore, the costs and time associated with each method should be evaluated. Shot blasting may be faster but potentially more expensive due to abrasive and energy consumption, while pickling may take more time but be more economical in terms of inputs. Finally, the specific application requirements, such as the desired surface roughness or corrosion tolerance, as well as compliance with safety regulations associated with each process, especially in handling chemicals in the case of pickling, must be considered.

Pillai et al., suggest that steels in the cold-drawn (CD) condition exhibit greater susceptibility to chloride corrosion compared to the same steels treated thermally by quenching and tempering, arguing that this is due to the impact on the passive film during the CD process [ 205 ]. However, it is essential to recognize that cold drawing offers significant advantages, such as improvements in mechanical properties, including increased tensile strength and yield strength, as well as better dimensional tolerance and superior surface finish. It is important to note that the argument by Pillai et al., may not fully reflect the context in which cold-drawn steel is used, as this process is specifically designed for manufacturing applications that require enhanced mechanical properties, rather than being a replacement for steel used in structural applications like rebar. This distinction is crucial for impartially evaluating the utility and characteristics of steel in different application environments.

Various methods have been presented, effective in reducing corrosion in sulfuric acid, offering fundamental mechanisms from film formation to advanced electrochemical processes aimed at controlling corrosion processes in detail. Lekbir et al., reported the effect of immersion and time for electrochemical processes using sulfuric acid in hot-dip galvanized processes [ 206 ]. Abdallah et al., suggested that the use of imidazole as an inhibitor achieves its effect on carbon steel, and that higher concentrations of imidazole make the inhibition more effective, preventing pitting on the surface of the steel [ 207 ]. Giovanardi et al., presented an electropickling method that completely removes oxides from the steel surface, restoring the overall appearance of the steel without causing damage [ 208 ]. Quraishi reported the inhibition mechanism in acids interacting with steel surfaces, focusing on the phenomenon of adsorption through valence forces and the variation in electron charge as they transition from one phase to another [ 209 ].

During the steel cleaning process with sulfuric acid, the temperature of the pickling tank is a very important factor. Maintaining a temperature close to 160°F will help eliminate scale and oxides, which will be easily removed with the subsequent rinsing. The sulfuric acid concentration should be between 9 and 12%, and the iron concentration should remain below 7%.

sections.heading: Heat treatment atmospheres
paragraphs: The selection of the heat treatment (HT) process should consider maintaining the mechanical integrity of the steel, protecting the surface, and ensuring the desired mechanical properties in low and medium carbon steels used in cold drawing (CD). Different types of HT offer advantages in controlling impurities, microstructural transformations, hydrogen reactions, and decarburization generation.

Carbon restoration using a methane-enriched atmosphere (CH4) is employed to reintroduce carbon into the surface of steel in cases where decarburization has occurred during heat treatments. During HT, methane gas decomposes into carbon and hydrogen gas (CH4 → C + 2H2), depositing on the steel surface and restoring previously lost carbon. The carburizing process is controlled by balancing the methane gas concentration in the atmosphere, the temperature, and the time. Special care must be taken to avoid over-carburizing, which could lead to undesirable brittleness and excess carbide formation.

There are also methane-endothermic atmospheres, generated by mixing the hydrocarbon with air in a special gas generator, followed by a controlled reaction at high temperature in the presence of a catalyst. This reaction involves the partial decomposition of methane: CH4 + O2 → CO + 2H2. This process generates a mixture of carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and nitrogen. It is ideal for controlling surface hardening without altering the steel's core and for introducing carbon into the steel surface. Unlike pure methane atmosphere, the gas mixture provides a balanced reducing environment for complex thermal processes where carburizing is required and surface protection is essential.

Ostwald et al., reported that water vapor produced by methane combustion leads to strong hydrogen absorption. They suggested that the use of dry air with oxygen content would form a protective layer on the steel, blocking hydrogen absorption [ 210 ].

The use of a propylene-enriched atmosphere (C3H6) during annealing acts as a reducing atmosphere and, when decomposed at high temperatures, releases hydrogen that reacts with the oxygen present, preventing the oxidation of the steel surface. This provides surface protection by minimizing the formation of surface oxides and avoiding carbon loss, thereby maintaining integrity and preventing surface decarburization. In an oxygen-free environment, it results in a bright surface finish after annealing, minimizing oxide formation.

Nitrogen (N) has also been used in atmospheres for heat treatments, aiming to prevent oxidation by displacing oxygen, which minimizes oxide formation and decarburization. It is a relatively economical gas ideal for industrial processes. In certain alloys containing Cr and V, nitrogen can react and form nitrides on the steel surface, resulting in a hard, wear-resistant layer, increasing durability and abrasion resistance. Furthermore, it is compatible with heat treatments such as quenching, tempering, and normalizing, providing a controlled atmosphere to protect the steel surface.

Hydrogen (H2) is a gas with highly reducing properties, which reacts with metallic oxides on the steel surface, reducing them to their pure metallic form and removing oxygen. This results in a clean, oxide-free surface, making it ideal for applications where surface quality is critical. It is primarily used in the Bright anneal process, as it removes surface contaminants. This process is ideal for improving formability and machinability. However, hydrogen requires strict use and precise control to avoid hydrogen embrittlement.

Plicht et al., identified a significant gap in the industry for heat treaters, highlighting the vital importance of providing operational flexibility along with better control over decarburization potential within atmospheric furnaces [ 211 ]. They suggest monitoring parameters for nitrogen–hydrogen atmospheres in heat treatment processes, focusing on stress relief and microstructure transformation, considering that conditions within furnace chambers change due to leaks, desorption impurities (such as moisture and lubricant decomposition). Part of this problem has been resolved by shifting from exothermic atmospheric processes to nitrogen and hydrogen atmospheres. A key indicator for detecting these issues is dew point measurement inside the furnace chamber. A very useful relationship for this monitoring is the partial pressure of moisture relative to the partial pressure of hydrogen. Advanced atmospheric monitoring systems, combined with a control system, represent an effective alternative for detecting significant process changes that require adjustments. For example, a controlled nitrogen–hydrogen gas flow system managed by a PLC, along with an oxygen probe to determine the moisture partial pressure value relative to the hydrogen partial pressure. This system has the potential to reduce operating costs and improve the quality of annealing. However, it should be noted that initial costs and operational complexity due to safety systems may complicate the process. Nevertheless, from an improvement perspective, nitrogen–hydrogen atmospheres are clean and stable, which will improve HT quality. The dew point measurement is crucial because it indicates the quality of the atmosphere and the presence of impurities.

The use of nitrogen and propylene-based atmospheres in industrial furnaces is an effective strategy for minimizing oxidation and decarburization during processes like annealing or stress relief. Propylene plays a crucial role by dissociating into carbon and hydrogen, generating a reducing atmosphere that reduces the partial oxygen pressure to controlled levels. This optimal balance, which avoids soot formation and ensures atmospheric stability, can be achieved through automated gas flow control based on advanced oxygen measurements in parts per billion, using specialized probes such as the Gold Probe or HP2000. Furthermore, implementing integrated control systems allows for dynamic adjustments of nitrogen and propylene flows based on thermal cycle conditions, optimizing the quality of treated parts. Additionally, cleaning cycles adapted to furnace design can be suggested, using controlled oxidation to remove soot deposits without compromising the integrity of internal components. Finally, identifying air leaks as the primary cause of decarburization highlights the importance of real-time monitoring with oxygen sensors to detect leaks and ensure an ideal atmosphere during heat treatment. This integrated approach combines advanced measurement technologies, automated control, and cleaning strategies to enhance the efficiency and quality of industrial thermal processes.

Yuan et al., reported the use of an argon atmosphere to avoid decarburization, following a sustained isotherm and then an austenitizing process, reporting the achievement of martensite when performing the quenching at room temperature [ 212 ]. Honkanen et al., reported the austenitization of a low-carbon steel followed by quenching, conducted in an air chamber, in a bed of carbon, and covering the sample with carbon powder to prevent decarboxylation [ 213 ]. Gordon et al., have reported the need to maintain certain compounds under inert atmospheres during the transformation process of the products [ 214 ]. Additionally, they have described the complexity of purging chambers when vapors from decomposition are introduced and explained the importance of eliminating long cleaning times for these chambers. Therefore, implementing inert atmospheres and optimizing purging processes represents a significant advantage for the production of high-quality steel.

Bacalhau et al., presented a study on SBQ bars of low-carbon steels, where it was observed that Ni delays the kinetic transformation of ferrite and pearlite, favoring the bainitic phase and the formation of martensite. It is important to highlight that the heat treatment was carried out in a vacuum atmosphere [ 215 ]. Seidman et al., have presented results on the redistribution of carbon according to variations in cooling rates, offering an explanation of the phase transformations that occur during the intercritical annealing treatment in a vacuum furnace (10⁻ 2  Torr). They reported using a Type K thermocouple to measure temperature, along with a contact dilatometer to monitor phase transformation. Two phases were identified: one of ferrite that coexists with austenite during intercritical annealing, and another ferrite phase that forms during cooling, with epitaxial grains [ 216 ].

Vacuum heat treatment is crucial to ensure that low- and medium-carbon steels meet critical specifications for decarburization and homogeneity, particularly in sensitive applications such as aerospace, which require more stringent control and precision. It is essential to ensure that no oxygen is present inside the chamber where the heat treatment occurs, as its presence can cause oxidation or decarburization. To achieve this, safety measures such as regular leak inspections and constant monitoring of critical process parameters are recommended. Key parameters include the recorded time when the vacuum begins, the pressure value indicated by the cold cathode channel, and the stabilization of the system before heating begins, ensuring that the leakage rate is below 10 microns per hour for low- and medium-carbon steels.

An adequate vacuum level, generally below 4 × 10⁻ 4  torr, is crucial to prevent stability issues in the process. If the leakage rate exceeds values higher than 10.5 × 10⁻ 4  torr, problems such as thermal gradients and loss of mechanical properties can arise. Additionally, an appropriate stabilization period is recommended to ensure uniform conditions and to record the chamber pressure at regular intervals during the treatment. Although some guidelines suggest not exceeding 25 microns per hour as a general leakage rate [ 1 ]. For low- and medium-carbon steels, it is recommended not to exceed 10 microns per hour, as higher values can cause issues with homogeneity in the treatment and compromise the quality of the treated material.

The success of the heat treatment process depends on the proper application of practices such as initial pumping (e.g., reducing the pressure to 1.0 × 10⁻ 4  torr or lower for one hour) and continuous monitoring using reliable measurement tools. For the design and improvement of these processes, it is useful to consider constitutive equations that describe the behavior of gases, heat transfer, and leakage rates, as these provide a solid scientific basis for predicting and controlling system performance [ 217 ,  218 ]. In this way, it is possible to ensure that the vacuum heat treatment meets quality requirements, avoiding decarburization and maximizing the microstructural uniformity of the treated steel.

sections.heading: Acoustic innovations in cold drawn (CD) steel and their impact on the cutting-edge SBQ steel market
paragraphs: Acoustics in steel are related to CD and the heat treatments applied, as these processes remodel and modify the microstructure, as well as the mechanical properties of the steel. This influences the propagation of acoustic waves through the material. The degree of anisotropy produced by CD affects the direction in which acoustic waves propagate. Due to the internal stresses and the anisotropy of the steel produced in CD, the speed of acoustic waves varies depending on the direction of propagation within the material, which is related to the preferential grain orientation and rolling direction. CD increases the hardness and strength of the material, which impacts the attenuation of acoustic waves, affecting how vibrations and sound dissipate within the steel. Hensman et al., have reported that an acoustic emission sensor can detect damage due to stress release related to events in a structure by detecting small amounts of energy, known as acoustic emissions [ 219 ]. In the aerospace industry, this is considered a life-saving measure. Schneider et al., have used acoustic waves to assess the surface of hardened steels, assuming that the speed of acoustic waves varies if the steel's microstructure has been hardened through martensitic transformation. They found that the backscattered electron amplitude reflects the fine-grained martensitic structure, and that the ultrasonic propagation speed is lower in martensitic steels than in annealed steels [ 220 ]. However, the material density and its stiffness are not considered. Different heat treatments can result in distinct phases, and even the grain size could alter the speed of acoustic waves. It is essential to emphasize the differentiation of residual stresses, as they also modify wave propagation. Although many variables exist, a gap in the industry becomes evident regarding how bainitic steels will respond to acoustic waves. Abdullah et al., have demonstrated how the acoustic emission technique in 1045 steels can be used to determine fatigue life. They mention that a high stress value contributes to a high average load, due to the high vibrational energy in the material, which explains the elevated amplitude of the acoustic emission signals [ 221 ]. However, it is necessary to clarify the limitations in correlating acoustic emission with fatigue life. First, the signal will not always be linear; internal variations in the steel's phase distribution can generate similar signals at different stages of fatigue. This approach would need to be complemented at least with a frequency or resonance analysis. Additionally, since energy can be absorbed by plastic deformation or in the form of heat, acoustic emission only detects a portion of the energy released in the form of elastic waves. Another drawback is its limited ability to discriminate between different types of defects. Grum et al., have studied the quenching process using acoustic emission to detect the phenomena occurring during immersion. They characterized the quenching process signature by recording it with a piezoelectric hydrophone [ 222 ]. A correlation was established between the acoustic emission (AE) signals and the mechanical properties, specifying that this correlation is nonlinear, and that the total elastic energy was omitted due to the sample's standard deviation. They concluded that AE is reliable for monitoring steel during the quenching process.

Riccioli et al., have reported the drawbacks of traditional NDT methods, such as magnetic particle inspection. While these methods can detect the length of discontinuities, they cannot measure the depth. On the other hand, AE allows for identifying, locating, and characterizing damage by monitoring transient stress waves. Some signals associated with failure modes in AE are characterized by having a low energy level, with an amplitude peak of less than 10 μV [ 223 ]. Seleznev et al., have developed a noise suppression algorithm aimed at detecting failures and correlating them with the characteristic signature in acoustic emission (AE) [ 224 ]. Notably, the AE activity in fractured samples was localized at the beginning of the cycle and was associated with the initiation of microcracks, while at the end of the fatigue life, the signal corresponded to crack propagation failure due to fatigue.

Heat treatments such as annealing and normalizing relieve internal stresses and homogenize the microstructure, reducing the anisotropy introduced by cold drawing, allowing acoustic waves to propagate uniformly throughout the material. These treatments partially restore ductility, which influences the speed and attenuation of the acoustic waves. A more uniform microstructure will enable consistent wave propagation.

During the quenching process, steel will harden, and its anisotropy increases, which is proportional to the propagation of acoustic waves. Harder steel will show a higher wave speed and at the same time higher attenuation. Toribio et al., have presented a study on the fracture behavior of steels, in which low plastic deformation (cold drawing degree < 3) was associated with a fracture surface contained within a transverse plane, showing isotropic fracture behavior for values below 3. In contrast, steels with high plastic deformation (≥ 3) exhibited fracture surfaces with different planes, indicating deviation in crack propagation and demonstrating anisotropic fracture behavior [ 225 ]. Toribio et al., present a fractographic analysis of a fatigue-fractured surface in a steel with a pearlitic microstructure, correlating the results with the micro-roughness of the surface [ 226 ,  227 ]. Gao et al., have presented a new ultrasonic testing method to characterize surface defects [ 228 ]. Cao et al., conducted a comparative study between two phenomenological damage models: the uncoupled B&M model and the coupled Lemaitre model [ 229 ].

Both models showed promising results in predicting ductile fractures. However, their analysis fails to consider that some of the metallic inclusions reported may be present in hot-rolled steel, which could influence crack nucleation and propagation. Additionally, it is important to note that most alloys produced through the cold drawing (CD) technique are not pearlitic, and the heat treatments applied to these alloys commonly involve processes such as spheroidizing or annealing, which significantly modify the microstructure and, consequently, the material's mechanical properties. Toribio et al., refer to how CD wire with a pearlitic microstructure is widely used in industrial applications [ 230 ]. However, pearlitic steel wire obtained through cold drawing (CD) actually represents less than 8% of the total volume of CD steel in the global SBQ market. More than 92% of the steel produced for CD applications is used for drawing into steel bars. This is a significant difference considering that the annealing processes used for bar processing in the CD industry do not produce pearlitic microstructures; in fact, they generate phases rich in ferrite and cementite, with a smaller percentage of lamellar pearlite. Therefore, the majority of CD steel applications worldwide involve bars where regular anneals—spheroidizing processes—soften the steel, optimizing it and allowing its movement through the phenomenon of flow stress when spheroidized steel is drawn through the die.

Non-destructive ultrasonic techniques in steel are dependent on the relationship between acoustics and heat treatment. When an internal defect is detected in steel, it largely depends on the material's acoustic homogeneity. In applications where steel is subjected to sources of vibration or cyclic loads, the hardness-acoustics-microstructure relationship is key to predicting performance under dynamic conditions. Shiraiwa et al., have validated that the acoustic emission technique and finite element analysis are effective for predicting failure modes. There is a clear correlation between the total acoustic emission energy and fracture ratio in fractured specimens, indicating that the amount of cold fracture in high-strength steels can be estimated from the total acoustic emission energy [ 231 ]. One of the drawbacks of this combination of techniques is that it may not be universal for all steels in their different heat treatment conditions. Therefore, it would first be necessary to have a database that analyzes the different types of steels and their conditions in order to compare and relate them.

Proverbio et al., have reported monitoring acoustic emission using a piezoelectric sensor with a bandwidth of 450 kHz, a resonance frequency of 150 kHz, and a capacitance of 350 pF. The results, presented as acoustic emission counts (AE counts) versus time, allow the identification of the moment of the first crack opening, i.e., the initiation time and the failure time [ 137 ]. These results show a strong dispersion and short periods of acoustic emission activity in the presence of cracks. Additionally, this information has been useful for identifying, along with fractography analysis, the direction of crack propagation and the failure mechanism. Acoustic emission (AE) monitoring has proven to be an effective technique for studying crack propagation. However, a more detailed analysis of the AE signals is required to better understand the micro-mechanisms driving crack propagation. Zuo et al., have reported that the time at which a crack occurs in steel when fractured during the quenching process can be detected by acoustic emission, using the clustering method to process the signals [ 232 ]. This approach is an improvement that helps the industry be better prepared to identify issues and prevent potential losses. Case et al., have reported that acoustic emission is applicable to cold drawing (CD) processes due to the physical mechanisms and how the material's frequency waves are affected once it is cold-drawn. They mention that the drawing speed, die temperature, and type of lubricant all have effects on the acoustic emission signals, resulting in higher signal amplitude [ 233 ]. This is beneficial in the cold drawing (CD) industry for the timely detection of issues in raw materials coming from hot rolling processes, where internal defects such as microcracks caused by inclusions are imperceptible. In heat treatment, the stress–strain curve of a material is modified by the thermal effect applied. This metallurgical change can be reflected by determining the residual stress, which can be measured directly using strain gauges [ 69 ].

sections.heading: Future Perspectives
paragraphs: Throughout this research, key areas for innovation have been identified that could drive the evolution of this field. Lubrication between steel bars and carbide dies stands out as one of the most important, focusing on the characterization of the lubricant and its mechanical behavior, evaluated from a friction perspective, as well as the use of nanometric compounds that could integrate new generations of chemical inputs. Another relevant parameter is the steel stretching speed, where further characterization of the flow stress in relation to the target geometry and drawing bench capabilities is still needed. Steel cleaning after heat treatment is another critical area; ensuring a scale-free surface could be achieved through innovative methods such as electrochemical techniques, which would reduce costs associated with processing time, labor, and the use of acids and chemical agents. Regarding the inspection and detection of internal cracks, the possibility of implementing acoustic emission techniques is proposed to identify defects proactively during the bar drawing process. As for heat treatments, efforts should focus on improving material quality by using thermocouples and advanced temperature monitoring sensors, as well as scientifically exploring gas mixtures for more precise control of advanced atmospheres. For induction hardening, it is recommended to optimize the control of hardening depth based on the quality of the microstructure and phase distribution resulting from cold work. This includes utilizing high-frequency technologies to improve energy efficiency, refining rapid and controlled cooling processes to optimize microstructures, and incorporating laser-guided cooling with inert gases. Finally, the potential of annealing is emphasized as the core of heat treatment through high-energy-efficient processes or via laser, steering these processes toward greater control and significant improvements in energy efficiency in cold drawing (CD). This comprehensive approach aims to advance towards a more efficient and sustainable industry.
